source.text: Ἄγουσιν οὖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ Καϊάφα εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον· ἦν δὲ πρωΐ· καὶ αὐτοὶ οὐκ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον, ἵνα μὴ μιανθῶσιν ἀλλὰ φάγωσιν τὸ πάσχα.

records.literal_gloss: They lead therefore the Jesus from the Caiaphas into the praetorium; it was now early; and they not entered into the praetorium, that not they might be defiled but might eat the Passover.

en.L: So they lead Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium. Now it was early. And they themselves did not enter into the praetorium, so that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.
en.B: Then they led Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They did not go into the headquarters themselves, to avoid becoming ritually unclean, since they wanted to eat the Passover.
en.R: Then they took Jesus from Caiaphas to the palace of the Roman governor. It was very early in the morning. The men who had brought {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} did not go inside the palace. They wanted to stay ritually clean so that they could eat the Passover meal.

decisions.choice: the praetorium: the headquarters of the Roman governor
decisions.reason: The word is a Latin military term taken into Greek. It was first a general's tent, then the residence and headquarters of a Roman governor (Matthew 27:27; Acts 23:35). The governor of Judea normally lived at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem at the great festivals. Whether his Jerusalem headquarters was the former palace of Herod the Great or the Antonia fortress beside the temple is not known for certain.

decisions.choice: early: the last part of the night, around dawn
decisions.reason: The word names the last of the four watches of the night, after the rooster crows (Mark 13:35); the rooster had just crowed (18:27). Jesus is brought to the governor at first light.

decisions.choice: defiled: made ritually unclean by entering a Gentile's dwelling
decisions.reason: The defilement is ritual, not moral. Jews held that going into the house of a Gentile made a person unclean (Acts 10:28; 11:3); later Jewish teaching, collected in the Mishnah, counts the dwellings of Gentiles as unclean (Oholot 18:7). A person who was unclean could not eat the Passover at its proper time (Numbers 9:6-13). John sets their care over ritual purity beside their pressing for an innocent man's death.

decisions.choice: eat the Passover: the Passover meal, still ahead on the day of the trial
alternatives: the festival offerings eaten during the following days of the feast
decisions.reason: In John the Passover meal has not yet been eaten when Jesus is tried and crucified: the day is "the day of Preparation of the Passover" (19:14), and the Sabbath that follows is "a great day" (19:31). In Matthew, Mark and Luke, the meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before was a Passover meal (Mark 14:12-16; Luke 22:15). The phrase can also mean the festival meals eaten during the seven days of the feast (compare 2 Chronicles 30:21-22), and on that reading the accounts agree in their timing. How they fit together is not settled here; the plain sense of John is followed.

decisions.choice: they: those who held Jesus at Caiaphas's house, the chief priests and their officers
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject; it carries on from 18:24-27. Pilate later says that the chief priests handed Jesus over (18:35), and the chief priests and their officers are the ones who shout for his crucifixion (19:6). "They themselves" sets these men, who stay outside, against Jesus, who is taken in.

decisions.choice: Historic present: they lead, says (L); led, said (B, R)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense to make them vivid ("they lead", "he says"). Literal keeps the present throughout this passage so that readers see the Greek form; Balanced and Readable use the past, the normal tense for telling a story in English. This decision covers every historic present in 18:28-40 (also "says" in 18:29 and 18:38).

decisions.choice: the governor's headquarters (B); the palace of the Roman governor (R)
decisions.reason: "Praetorium" is a Latin word few readers know, so Balanced and Readable say what the building was (meaning decision m1). Readable names the governor as Roman, since the story turns on the difference between the Jewish authorities and the Roman court. Verse 33 uses the same words.

decisions.choice: to avoid becoming ritually unclean (B); the men who had brought him, stay ritually clean, the Passover meal (R)
alternatives: so that they would not be defiled
decisions.reason: "Defiled" could be taken as moral corruption, so Balanced and Readable say it was a matter of ritual cleanness (meaning decision m3). Readable names the subject as the men who had brought Jesus, without saying more than the text (meaning decision m5), and says "meal" for the Passover (meaning decision m4).

source.text: ἐξῆλθεν οὖν ὁ Πιλᾶτος ἔξω πρὸς αὐτοὺς καὶ φησίν· Τίνα κατηγορίαν φέρετε κατὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τούτου;

records.literal_gloss: Went out therefore the Pilate outside to them and says, "What accusation do you bring against the man this?"

en.L: So Pilate went out to them and says, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
en.B: So Pilate came outside to them and asked, "What charge are you making against this man?"
en.R: So Pilate came out to meet them. "What do you accuse this man of?" he asked.

decisions.choice: Pilate: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36 (Luke 3:1). A stone inscription found at Caesarea in 1961 calls him "prefect of Judea". John brings him into the story without introduction, as a figure his readers knew. Only the governor could order an execution (18:31).

decisions.choice: went out ... outside: the scene moves between the courtyard outside and the headquarters inside
decisions.reason: Because the accusers will not come in (18:28), Pilate goes back and forth: out to them here, in to Jesus (18:33), out again (18:38), in (19:9), out (19:4, 13). The doubled "went out outside" marks the first move. The questioning of Jesus happens inside; the shouting happens outside.

decisions.choice: accusation: a formal charge brought before a judge
decisions.reason: The word is a legal one. Pilate opens a hearing in proper form by asking for the charge.

decisions.choice: What charge are you making (B); What do you accuse this man of (R)
decisions.reason: Plain modern words for the legal question (meaning decision m3). The historic present "says" is covered by decision r-en-1 at 18:28.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθησαν καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Εἰ μὴ ἦν οὗτος κακὸν ποιῶν, οὐκ ἄν σοι παρεδώκαμεν αὐτόν.

records.literal_gloss: They answered and said to him, "If not was this [man] evil doing, not [would] to you we have handed over him."

en.L: They answered and said to him, "If this [man] were not doing evil, we would not have handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to you."
en.B: They answered, "We would not have handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to you if this man were not a wrongdoer."
en.R: "He is a criminal," they answered. "If {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} were not, we would not have handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to you."

decisions.choice: were not doing evil: a man who habitually does wrong, a wrongdoer
decisions.reason: The verb "to be" with the participle "doing" describes an ongoing practice. They name no crime. Pilate asked for a charge (18:29); they answer that their own handing over should be proof enough.

decisions.choice: handed over: the word used again and again for Jesus's betrayal and surrender
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of Judas (18:2, 5), of the chief priests (18:35), of what Jesus' servants would have prevented (18:36), and of Pilate himself (19:16). It traces the chain by which Jesus is passed from hand to hand to the cross.

decisions.choice: handed over, at every level
decisions.reason: One English phrase is kept for this verb through the passion story so that readers can follow the chain (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: We would not have handed him over to you if this man were not a wrongdoer (B); He is a criminal ... If he were not (R)
alternatives: If this man were not doing evil (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the main clause first and uses a noun for the ongoing practice (meaning decision m1). Readable states the claim first in a short sentence; it says no more than "doing evil" implies.

source.text: εἶπεν οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Λάβετε αὐτὸν ὑμεῖς, καὶ κατὰ τὸν νόμον ὑμῶν κρίνατε αὐτόν.

records.literal_gloss: Said therefore to them the Pilate, "Take him you, and according to the law of you judge him."

en.L: So Pilate said to them, "You take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and judge {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} according to your law."
en.B: So Pilate told them, "You take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, then, and try {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} under your own law."
en.R: Pilate said to them, "Take {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away and put {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} on trial yourselves, by your own law."

decisions.choice: you take him: the stressed "you" pushes the case back to them
decisions.reason: "You" is added in Greek where it is not needed, which stresses it. Since they have named no crime against Roman law, Pilate tells them to deal with the man themselves.

decisions.choice: your law: the Law of Moses, applied in the Jewish courts
decisions.reason: Rome let the peoples it ruled settle many matters by their own laws and courts. In Judea the high priest and the council judged cases under the Law of Moses. Pilate treats the matter as an internal religious dispute.

decisions.choice: judge: try in court and give a verdict
decisions.reason: The verb has its legal sense here, as in 7:51 ("Does our law judge a man without first hearing him?").

decisions.choice: try (B); put on trial (R)
decisions.reason: In modern English "judge" can mean simply to form an opinion of someone; "try" makes the court setting plain (meaning decision m3).

source.text: εἶπον αὐτῷ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔξεστιν ἀποκτεῖναι οὐδένα·

records.literal_gloss: Said to him the Jews, "For us not it is lawful to kill anyone";

en.L: The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
en.B: The Jewish leaders replied, "We are not permitted to execute anyone."
en.R: But the Jewish leaders answered, "We are not allowed to put anyone to death."

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers who brought Jesus to Pilate
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: They are the ones who led Jesus from Caiaphas (18:28) and who, Pilate says, handed him over (18:35); at 19:6 the chief priests and their officers shout for his death. The word names this group of leaders, not the people: Jesus and his disciples are Jews, and so are many who believed in him (11:45; 12:11).

decisions.choice: not lawful for us: under Roman rule only the governor could order a man's death
alternatives: it was not lawful to execute anyone during the festival
it was not lawful for them to crucify
decisions.reason: When Rome took direct rule of Judea in AD 6, Josephus says the first governor was sent with power over life and death (Jewish War 2.117). Some events seem to go against this: the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7:58), and the execution of James the Lord's brother in AD 62 while there was no governor in the province, for which the high priest was removed from office (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200-203). So the rule may have had exceptions, or such killings may have been unlawful. John's point is plain either way: they need Pilate to sentence Jesus.

decisions.choice: the answer shows that they want a death sentence, not a trial
decisions.reason: Pilate offered them a trial under their own law; their reply shows that they have already decided on death. "For us" is put first for stress: they cannot do it, Pilate can. The purpose clause of verse 32 hangs on this exchange.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: not permitted to execute (B); not allowed to put to death (R)
decisions.reason: "Kill" here means a lawful execution after a sentence, not murder (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἵνα ὁ λόγος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πληρωθῇ ὃν εἶπεν σημαίνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ ἤμελλεν ἀποθνῄσκειν.

records.literal_gloss: that the word of the Jesus might be fulfilled which he said signifying by what kind of death he was about to die.

en.L: [This was] so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spoke, signifying by what kind of death {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was about to die.
en.B: This was so that the word Jesus had spoken would be fulfilled, the word that showed what kind of death {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was going to die.
en.R: This happened so that what Jesus had said would come true. He had pointed to the kind of death {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was going to die: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would be lifted up on a cross.

decisions.choice: the word of Jesus: his saying about being lifted up (12:32-33; compare 3:14; 8:28)
alternatives: a saying about being handed over to the Gentiles (Mark 10:33)
decisions.reason: The words "signifying by what kind of death he was about to die" repeat 12:33 exactly, where John explained Jesus's saying "when I am lifted up from the earth". Death by Jewish sentence would have been by stoning (8:59; 10:31); because Jesus is handed to the Roman governor, he will die by the Roman penalty of crucifixion, raised up on a cross.

decisions.choice: so that ... might be fulfilled: what happens carries out what Jesus foretold
decisions.reason: John uses this language for Scripture being fulfilled (12:38; 13:18; 19:24, 36), and here, as at 18:9, for Jesus's own words. The authorities' refusal to try Jesus themselves leads, beyond their intent, to the death he had already named.

decisions.choice: signifying: indicating by a hint, not saying outright
decisions.reason: The verb means to point to something by a sign. Jesus had spoken in a picture ("lifted up"), not in plain words, as at 12:33 and 21:19.

decisions.choice: [This was] (L); This was (B); This happened (R); he would be lifted up on a cross (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek purpose clause hangs on the exchange in verse 31; English needs a main clause, so every level supplies one, Literal in brackets. Readable also says what kind of death was meant, as at 12:33 (meaning decision m1). The narrator, not a character, gives the explanation.

source.text: Εἰσῆλθεν οὖν πάλιν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον ὁ Πιλᾶτος καὶ ἐφώνησεν τὸν Ἰησοῦν καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων;

records.literal_gloss: Entered therefore again into the praetorium the Pilate and called the Jesus and said to him, "You are the king of the Jews?"

en.L: So Pilate entered again into the praetorium and called Jesus and said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the King of the Jews?"
en.B: Then Pilate went back inside the headquarters. He called Jesus to him and asked, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the King of the Jews?"
en.R: Pilate went back into the palace and called for Jesus. He asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the King of the Jews?"

decisions.choice: the Jews, in the title: the Jewish nation
decisions.reason: "King of the Jews" is a title for the ruler of the nation, the people as a whole. Rome had given it to Herod the Great (Josephus, Antiquities 14.385), and in the Gospels it is used by Gentiles (Matthew 2:2; John 19:3, 19), while Jews say "King of Israel" (1:49; 12:13). Here the word does not mean the authorities, and the title keeps "the Jews".

decisions.choice: the political charge: claiming to be king without Rome's leave
alternatives: a religious question about the Messiah
decisions.reason: Pilate's first question shows the charge the accusers had brought: that Jesus claimed to be king. Under Rome only a ruler appointed by Rome could hold that title, so the claim was rebellion against Caesar (19:12, 15). Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for rebels, and the charge was written above the cross (19:19).

decisions.choice: you: stressed, perhaps with surprise
decisions.reason: The pronoun is placed first and is not needed in Greek. Pilate may be expressing disbelief that this bound prisoner could claim a throne; the same question opens Jesus's trial before Pilate in all four Gospels (Matthew 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3).

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews, at every level
alternatives: the King of the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: This is a title naming the nation (meaning decision m1), so every level keeps the words John wrote, here and at 18:39, with no footnote. "King" takes a capital as part of a title. "Headquarters" (B) and "palace" (R) follow decision r-en-2 at 18:28.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς· Ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ σὺ τοῦτο λέγεις ἢ ἄλλοι εἶπόν σοι περὶ ἐμοῦ;

records.literal_gloss: Answered Jesus, "From yourself you this say, or others told you about me?"

en.L: Jesus answered, "Do you say this from yourself, or did others tell you about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.B: Jesus answered, "Are you asking this on your own, or have others told you about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.R: Jesus replied, "Is that your own question? Or did other people tell you this about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

decisions.choice: from yourself: on your own account, from your own thinking
decisions.reason: The phrase means acting or speaking on one's own initiative, as when Jesus says he does nothing "from himself" (5:19; 7:17) and John says Caiaphas did not speak "from himself" (11:51).

decisions.choice: Jesus asks whose question it is, and so what kind of king is meant
decisions.reason: If the question is Pilate's own, "king" means a rebel against Rome; if it comes from the accusers, it carries their charge, and behind it Israel's hope of an anointed king. Jesus does not deny being a king (18:36-37), but he will not accept the title in the sense of a rival to Caesar. This reading of his purpose is likely from what follows but is not stated.

decisions.choice: asking this on your own (B); your own question (R)
decisions.reason: The idiom "from yourself" is put in plain words (meaning decision m1); Pilate has asked a question, so Balanced and Readable say "asking" and "question". "You" here is Pilate and takes no setting.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Μήτι ἐγὼ Ἰουδαῖός εἰμι;

records.literal_gloss: Answered the Pilate, "Not I a Jew am?"

en.L: Pilate answered, "I am not a Jew, am I?"
en.B: Pilate answered, "Do you think I am a Jew?"
en.R: Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? No!"

decisions.choice: a scornful question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The question word expects "no", often with impatience, and "I" is stressed. Pilate rejects the idea that he would have any interest of his own in Jewish questions about a king.

decisions.choice: Jew: a member of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: Here the word means the people as a whole, set against Pilate, a Roman and a Gentile. It needs no footnote, since every level keeps it.

decisions.choice: Do you think I am a Jew? (B); Am I a Jew? No! (R)
alternatives: I am not a Jew, am I? (Literal)
decisions.reason: English shows the expected answer and the scorn in different ways (meaning decision m1): Balanced turns it to Jesus with "Do you think", and Readable gives the answer the Greek implies.

source.text: τὸ ἔθνος τὸ σὸν καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς παρέδωκάν σε ἐμοί· τί ἐποίησας;

records.literal_gloss: The nation the yours and the chief priests handed over you to me; what did you do?

en.L: Your own nation and the chief priests handed {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} over to me. What did {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do?
en.B: Your own nation and the chief priests are the ones who handed {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} over to me. What have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} done?
en.R: It was your own nation and the chief priests who handed {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} over to me. What did {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} do?

decisions.choice: your nation: Israel as a nation, acting through its rulers
alternatives: every member of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: The word is the one the chief priests and Caiaphas use for the nation they rule and claim to protect (11:48-52). In Pilate's mouth it means the nation in its official leadership; the ones he names, and the only ones present in the scene, are the chief priests and those with them (18:28; 19:6). Pilate's words do not say that the Jewish people as a whole handed Jesus over, and John does not say so either.

decisions.choice: your own: the possessive is stressed
decisions.reason: The nation is put first and the possessive is added after it for stress: Jesus's own people, not Rome, brought the case. It answers Jesus's question whether others had told Pilate about him (18:34).

decisions.choice: what did you do: Pilate asks for the actual offense
decisions.reason: Pilate leaves the title aside and asks what Jesus has done, since the accusers named no crime (18:30). Jesus answers about his kingdom instead (18:36).

decisions.choice: your own nation; handed over, at every level
decisions.reason: "Nation" keeps the word Pilate used, the word the leaders used of the people they govern (meaning decision m1), so that no level makes it a statement about the whole people. "Handed over" follows decision r-en-1 at 18:30.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς· Ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου· εἰ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου ἦν ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμή, οἱ ὑπηρέται οἱ ἐμοὶ ἠγωνίζοντο ἄν, ἵνα μὴ παραδοθῶ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις· νῦν δὲ ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐντεῦθεν.

records.literal_gloss: Answered Jesus, "The kingdom the mine not is of the world this; if of the world this were the kingdom the mine, the attendants the mine would have been fighting, that not I might be handed over to the Jews; but now the kingdom the mine not is from here."

en.L: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} kingdom were of this world, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} attendants would be fighting, so that I might not be handed over to the Jews. But now {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} kingdom is not from here."
en.B: Jesus answered, "My kingdom does not come from this world. If it did, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servants would be fighting to keep {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} from being handed over to the Jewish leaders. But as it is, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} kingdom is not from here."
en.R: Jesus answered, "My kingdom does not come from this world. If it did, those who serve {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} would fight to keep {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} from being handed over to the Jewish leaders. But {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} kingdom is not from here."

decisions.choice: not of this world: his kingdom does not have its origin or its authority from this world
alternatives: his kingdom has nothing to do with this world
his kingdom is only spiritual or only future
decisions.reason: "Of" here means coming from, as when Jesus says his disciples are not "of the world" (17:14, 16) though they are in it. His kingship does not rest on the world's power or rise from it; it comes from above (3:31). The closing words "not from here" say the same thing again. "The world" here is humanity in its life apart from God and against him (15:18-19).

decisions.choice: attendants: men who serve under a ruler and act for him, such as guards or officers
decisions.reason: The word is not the one for a slave. It is the word for the officers sent by the chief priests to arrest Jesus (7:32; 18:3, 12) and who struck him (18:22). Jesus says that if his kingdom were the world's kind, he too would have armed men acting for him. Peter's sword was drawn and put away (18:10-11).

decisions.choice: the Jews: the authorities who had Jesus arrested and brought him to Pilate
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of those into whose hands he would have been delivered, the chief priests and their officers who arrested him (18:3, 12) and handed him to Pilate (18:35). He is himself a Jew, and so are the servants he speaks of; the word names the authorities, not the people.

decisions.choice: but now: but as things are, not "at this time"
alternatives: but at present (implying that later it will be from here)
decisions.reason: After an unreal "if", "now" marks the real state of affairs, as in 8:40 and 9:41. It does not hint that the kingdom will become of this world later.

decisions.choice: kingdom: his kingship and rule, not only a territory
decisions.reason: The word means reign and royal power as well as the realm ruled. Jesus answers Pilate's question about whether he is a king (18:33) by speaking of his reign. Apart from 3:3 and 3:5 this is the only place the word occurs in John.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: attendants (L); servants (B); those who serve me (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the narrow sense, men who serve under someone (meaning decision m2). "Servants" is used at Balanced as a natural word for those who act for a king; it is not used here for the word for a slave, which this passage does not have. Readable uses an everyday phrase. "Officers" or "guards" would make Jesus speak of a force he did not have.

decisions.choice: does not come from this world; If it did (B, R); as it is (B)
decisions.reason: "Of this world" can be heard as "has nothing to do with this world"; "come from" gives the sense of origin (meaning decision m1). The repeated phrase is shortened to "If it did". "As it is" gives the sense of "now" (meaning decision m4).

source.text: εἶπεν οὖν αὐτῷ ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Οὐκοῦν βασιλεὺς εἶ σύ;

records.literal_gloss: Said therefore to him the Pilate, "So then a king are you?"

en.L: So Pilate said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "So then, a king are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"
en.B: Pilate said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "So {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are a king after all?"
en.R: Then Pilate said, "So {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are a king?"

decisions.choice: So then: a question that draws a conclusion from what Jesus has said
alternatives: an exclamation: "So you are a king!"
decisions.reason: The word marks an inference. Jesus has spoken of "my kingdom" three times (18:36), and Pilate seizes on it. The SBLGNT prints it as a question; it may carry irony.

decisions.choice: a king: without "the"; Pilate no longer says "the King of the Jews"
decisions.reason: Pilate's first question named a title (18:33); now he asks only whether Jesus claims to be a king of any kind. "You" comes last and is stressed.

decisions.choice: after all (B)
decisions.reason: Shows that Pilate draws a conclusion from what Jesus has just said (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Σὺ λέγεις ὅτι βασιλεύς εἰμι.

records.literal_gloss: Answered the Jesus, "You say that a king I am."

en.L: Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king."
en.B: Jesus answered, "You are the one who says that I am a king."
en.R: Jesus answered, "It is you who say that I am a king."

decisions.choice: You say that I am a king: a yes, but with a reservation about the word
alternatives: a plain yes: "You say rightly that I am a king"
You say it, because I am a king
decisions.reason: The Gospels use the same short answer before the high priest and before Pilate (Matthew 26:64; 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3). It does not deny the claim, and Jesus goes on to speak of his kingship; but it leaves the word on Pilate's lips, since Pilate means something Jesus does not. The little word after "say" can also be read as "because", making a firmer yes: "You say so, because I am a king." The evidence does not settle how strong the yes is, so every level keeps the words open.

decisions.choice: You are the one who says (B); It is you who say (R)
decisions.reason: "You" is stressed in Greek. Balanced and Readable show the stress without turning the answer into a plain yes or a plain no (meaning decision m1). "You" here is Pilate and takes no setting.

source.text: ἐγὼ εἰς τοῦτο γεγέννημαι καὶ εἰς τοῦτο ἐλήλυθα εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἵνα μαρτυρήσω τῇ ἀληθείᾳ· πᾶς ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀκούει μου τῆς φωνῆς.

records.literal_gloss: I for this have been born and for this have come into the world, that I might testify to the truth; everyone the [one] being of the truth hears my the voice.

en.L: For this I have been born, and for this I have come into the world, that I might testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} voice.
en.B: I was born for this, and I came into the world for this: to testify to the truth. All who belong to the truth listen to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} voice.
en.R: This is why I was born, and this is why I came into the world: to be a witness to the truth. All who belong to the truth listen to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: born ... come into the world: his human birth and his coming from God
alternatives: two ways of saying only that he was born
decisions.reason: "I" is stressed. In John, coming into the world is said of one who comes from God (3:19; 6:14; 11:27; 16:28). Jesus speaks of a purpose that goes back before his birth. Pilate hears only the first half.

decisions.choice: testify to the truth: bear witness to God's reality, made known in Jesus
decisions.reason: In John the truth is what God is and what he has made known in his Son (1:14, 17; 8:32; 14:6). Jesus speaks of his kingship in terms of witness, not force: this is how he reigns. Testimony is a thread through the Gospel (1:7; 3:11; 5:31-39).

decisions.choice: of the truth: belonging to the truth, having one's life from it
decisions.reason: "Of" names belonging and origin, as in "whoever is of God hears the words of God" (8:47). Those who belong to the truth recognize Jesus's voice, as his sheep know the voice of the shepherd (10:3-4, 16, 27). Without saying so, Jesus invites Pilate to listen.

decisions.choice: testify (L, B); be a witness to (R); hears my voice (L); listen to my voice (B); listen to me (R)
decisions.reason: "Testify" is used for this verb through John. Hearing here means listening and responding (meaning decision m3), so Balanced says "listen to". Readable drops "voice" for plain speech; the echo of the shepherd's voice (10:3-4) remains at Literal and Balanced.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Τί ἐστιν ἀλήθεια;

records.literal_gloss: Says to him the Pilate, "What is truth?"

decisions.choice: truth: without "the", truth in general
decisions.reason: Jesus spoke of "the truth" he came to testify to (18:37); Pilate asks about truth as an idea. The two are speaking past each other.

decisions.choice: the tone of Pilate's question is not stated
decisions.reason: John does not say how Pilate meant it, and Pilate does not wait for an answer; he goes straight out (18:38b). The reader of the Gospel already knows the answer Jesus has given: "I am the way and the truth and the life" (14:6).

source.text: Καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν πάλιν ἐξῆλθεν πρὸς τοὺς Ἰουδαίους, καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἐγὼ οὐδεμίαν εὑρίσκω ἐν αὐτῷ αἰτίαν·

records.literal_gloss: And this having said again he went out to the Jews, and says to them, "I no find in him case";

en.L: And having said this, he went out again to the Jews, and says to them, "I find no case in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.B: After saying this, he went back out to the Jewish leaders and told them, "I find no case against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.R: After saying this, Pilate went out again to the Jewish leaders. He told them, "I find no reason to condemn {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers waiting outside
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: They are the same group who would not enter the headquarters (18:28) and who brought the charge (18:29-31, 35). John mentions no crowd in the trial; when he names the ones who shout, they are the chief priests and their officers (19:6). Others may have been with them, but the word here names the accusers, not the people.

decisions.choice: case: a legal ground for a charge
decisions.reason: The word means the cause or ground of an accusation. As judge, Pilate finds nothing in Jesus that would support a charge under Roman law. He will say so again twice (19:4, 6).

decisions.choice: I: stressed, the judge's own finding
decisions.reason: Pilate sets his finding as judge against what the accusers claim (18:30).

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: no case against him (B); no reason to condemn him (R)
decisions.reason: Pilate speaks as a judge, so Balanced and Readable use the language of a court (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἔστιν δὲ συνήθεια ὑμῖν ἵνα ἕνα ἀπολύσω ὑμῖν ἐν τῷ πάσχα· βούλεσθε οὖν ἀπολύσω ὑμῖν τὸν βασιλέα τῶν Ἰουδαίων;

records.literal_gloss: Is but a custom for you that one I release to you at the Passover; do you want therefore I release to you the king of the Jews?"

en.L: But you have a custom that I release one [man] to you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
en.B: But you have a custom that I set one prisoner free for you at the Passover. So shall I set the King of the Jews free for you?"
en.R: But you have a custom. At Passover I set one prisoner free for you. So do you want me to free the King of the Jews?"

decisions.choice: a custom of releasing one prisoner at Passover
decisions.reason: All four Gospels speak of this custom (Matthew 27:15; Mark 15:6; Luke 23:18). No other ancient source mentions such a release in Judea, though rulers elsewhere did sometimes free prisoners at festivals. Pilate calls it "your" custom: a favor to the people at their feast of freedom from slavery in Egypt.

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews: the title of the charge, the Jewish nation
decisions.reason: As at 18:33, the title names the nation. In Pilate's mouth it may be mocking, aimed at the accusers as much as at Jesus (19:14-15).

decisions.choice: one: one prisoner
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "one"; the context shows that a prisoner is meant. "You" throughout is plural, the people outside.

decisions.choice: one [man] (L); one prisoner, set free (B, R)
decisions.reason: English needs a noun for "one" (meaning decision m3). "King of the Jews" is kept at every level, as at 18:33 (decision r-en-1 there).

source.text: ἐκραύγασαν οὖν πάλιν λέγοντες· Μὴ τοῦτον ἀλλὰ τὸν Βαραββᾶν.

records.literal_gloss: They shouted therefore again saying, "Not this [one] but the Barabbas."

en.L: So they shouted again, saying, "Not this [man], but Barabbas!"
en.B: At that they shouted again, "Not this one! Barabbas!"
en.R: They shouted back again, "Not this man! Give us Barabbas!"

decisions.choice: again: though John has told of no earlier shouting
alternatives: an earlier outcry the reader is meant to assume
decisions.reason: John has not mentioned any shouting before this. "Again" may assume that the accusers had already been loud in their demands, or may mean simply "in turn". It does not change what they said.

decisions.choice: shouted: cried out loudly
decisions.reason: The same verb describes the crowd's "Hosanna" at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem (12:13) and the shouts of "Crucify!" (19:6, 15).

decisions.choice: Barabbas: an Aramaic name meaning "son of the father"
decisions.reason: John does not explain the name, and he does not say who Barabbas was until the next sentence. The name was an ordinary one; any wordplay with Jesus as the Son of the Father is not drawn out by John.

decisions.choice: Not this one! Barabbas! (B); Not this man! Give us Barabbas! (R)
decisions.reason: A shout is short, so Balanced breaks it in two. Readable supplies "Give us" to make plain what they want.

records.literal_gloss: Was now the Barabbas a bandit.

decisions.choice: bandit: a violent robber, possibly a rebel against Rome
decisions.reason: The word is the one used in 10:1 and 10:8 for the bandit who climbs into the sheepfold. It means a robber who uses violence, and in the first century it was also used of armed men who rose against Roman rule. Mark 15:7 and Luke 23:19 say that Barabbas was in prison for an uprising and for murder, so he may have been such a rebel.

decisions.choice: the closing remark: the people's choice set beside the shepherd and the king
decisions.reason: John ends the scene with four words. The man chosen is the kind Jesus named in 10:1, 8 as the opposite of the good shepherd, and a man of violence is preferred to a king whose servants do not fight (18:36). The irony is left unspoken.

decisions.choice: bandit, at every level
decisions.reason: The same English word as in 10:1 and 10:8, so that readers can hear the echo (meaning decision m2). The footnote gives "rebel" (meaning decision m1).
